pharm: Long-acting non-depolarizing aminosteroid neuromuscular blocker that competitively antagonizes acetylcholine at the motor end-plate nicotinic receptors, producing skeletal muscle relaxation to facilitate intubation and surgery; minimal cardiovascular effects.
tags: Renal elimination - prolonged in renal failure
quick: Intubation: 70-85 mcg/kg IV (typical 50-100 mcg/kg); maintenance 10-15 mcg/kg
Use only if clearly needed; can cross placenta - monitor neonate
Caution; limited data - generally a single perioperative exposure
Reduce dose / avoid - renally eliminated, markedly prolonged block
Use with caution; effect may be prolonged
Peripheral nerve stimulation (train-of-four), ventilation, neuromuscular recovery
summary: Pipecuronium bromide is a long-acting, non-depolarizing aminosteroid neuromuscular blocking agent used as an adjunct to general anesthesia to facilitate tracheal intubation and to provide skeletal muscle relaxation during surgery or mechanical ventilation. It competitively blocks acetylcholine at the nicotinic receptors of the neuromuscular junction, causing flaccid paralysis. It is intended for use only by clinicians experienced in airway management and neuromuscular blockade, in settings with facilities for intubation, mechanical ventilation, and oxygen, because it produces no analgesia, sedation, or loss of consciousness and must be accompanied by adequate anesthesia/sedation. It is notable for minimal cardiovascular effects (little vagolytic activity or histamine release) compared with some other agents, making it suitable when hemodynamic stability is desired. It is eliminated primarily by the kidneys, so its effect is significantly prolonged in renal impairment; effects are also prolonged by conditions and drugs that potentiate neuromuscular blockade. Residual block is reversed with an anticholinesterase (e.g., neostigmine) plus an antimuscarinic, guided by neuromuscular monitoring. The branded product (Arduan) has limited current marketing in the United States.
indications: Adjunct to general anesthesia to facilitate endotracheal intubation
Provision of skeletal muscle relaxation during surgery
Facilitation of mechanical ventilation in anesthetized/intubated patients requiring prolonged muscle relaxation

dosage.n: Provides conditions for intubation; onset is dose-dependent. Reduce if used after succinylcholine
Incremental doses provide ~about 50 minutes of additional block

dosage.d: Reduce dose (initial ~50 mcg/kg or less) and titrate
dosage.n: Markedly prolonged effect; avoid if possible or use with close monitoring

dosage.d: Base dose on ideal/lean body weight

admin: For use only by or under the direct supervision of clinicians experienced in the use of neuromuscular blocking agents and management of the airway
Administer by intravenous injection only, with facilities for intubation, mechanical ventilation, oxygen, and reversal agents immediately available
Always provide adequate anesthesia and analgesia/sedation - this drug causes paralysis but no loss of consciousness or pain relief
Use a peripheral nerve stimulator (train-of-four monitoring) to guide dosing and confirm adequate recovery before extubation
Reverse residual block when appropriate with an anticholinesterase (e.g., neostigmine) given with an antimuscarinic (e.g., atropine/glycopyrrolate)
moa: Pipecuronium is a non-depolarizing (competitive) neuromuscular blocking agent of the aminosteroid class. It binds competitively to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane of the motor end-plate, preventing acetylcholine released from the motor nerve terminal from binding and depolarizing the membrane. This blockade of neuromuscular transmission produces a flaccid paralysis of skeletal muscle without an initial depolarization (no fasciculations). The block is dose-dependent and, being competitive, can be antagonized by increasing acetylcholine concentration at the junction, which is the basis for reversal with acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as neostigmine. Pipecuronium has little or no vagolytic or ganglion-blocking activity and does not cause clinically significant histamine release, accounting for its relatively stable cardiovascular profile.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to pipecuronium bromide or the bromide ion
Use without facilities and personnel for tracheal intubation and controlled mechanical ventilation
relative: Significant renal impairment (markedly prolonged block - avoid or reduce dose)
Myasthenia gravis and other neuromuscular diseases (extreme sensitivity)
Concomitant drugs that potentiate neuromuscular blockade (e.g., aminoglycosides, magnesium)
Conditions altering response: hypothermia, dehydration, obesity
monitor: Depth of neuromuscular blockade by peripheral nerve stimulation (train-of-four)
Recovery of neuromuscular function before extubation
Adequacy of concurrent anesthesia/sedation and analgesia

preg: There are no adequate well-controlled studies in pregnant women; use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. Neuromuscular blockers cross the placenta to a limited extent; when used (e.g., for cesarean section), monitor the neonate for muscle weakness and respiratory depression and have neonatal resuscitation available.
lact: It is not known whether pipecuronium is excreted in human milk. As it is typically administered as a single perioperative dose and is highly ionized with rapid clearance in patients with normal renal function, significant infant exposure is unlikely, but caution is advised.
renal: Pipecuronium is eliminated predominantly by the kidneys, so renal impairment substantially prolongs and intensifies neuromuscular blockade and delays recovery. Avoid where possible; if used, reduce the dose, titrate carefully against neuromuscular monitoring, and anticipate a prolonged effect and the need for ventilatory support.
hepatic: Hepatic impairment and biliary obstruction may alter distribution and prolong the duration of action. Use with caution, reduce dosing as needed, and monitor neuromuscular function closely.

major: Aminoglycoside and polypeptide antibiotics (e.g., gentamicin, polymyxins, clindamycin) - potentiate and prolong neuromuscular blockade
Magnesium salts (e.g., in pre-eclampsia) - markedly enhance and prolong blockade
Volatile/inhalational anesthetics (e.g., isoflurane, sevoflurane, enflurane) - potentiate neuromuscular block
moderate: Other neuromuscular blockers, including prior succinylcholine - altered (often potentiated) effect
Loop and thiazide diuretics, and other drugs causing hypokalemia - potentiate blockade
Local anesthetics, quinidine, calcium channel blockers, lithium - may enhance blockade
Corticosteroids with prolonged neuromuscular blockade - risk of myopathy/prolonged weakness
minor: Anticonvulsants (chronic phenytoin/carbamazepine) - may cause resistance to the block, requiring higher doses
interactions.alcohol: Not applicable for single perioperative administration.
interactions.diagnostics: No specific laboratory interference; monitor electrolytes, as imbalances alter the degree of blockade.

serious: Prolonged respiratory depression/apnea due to residual paralysis
Profound, prolonged blockade in renal impairment
rare: Myopathy/prolonged weakness with concomitant corticosteroids and prolonged use
emergency: Anaphylaxis (bronchospasm, hypotension, swelling, cardiovascular collapse) during anesthesia
Inability to breathe adequately after the agent due to prolonged or residual paralysis
Cardiac arrhythmia or severe hemodynamic instability

monitoring: Continuous monitoring of neuromuscular function with a peripheral nerve stimulator (train-of-four) to titrate dosing and confirm recovery
Adequacy of ventilation and oxygenation throughout and after the procedure
Cardiovascular monitoring (heart rate, blood pressure, ECG)
Recovery of adequate neuromuscular strength before extubation and after reversal
Renal function and electrolytes, which affect duration of blockade
counsel: This medicine is given by an anesthesia team during surgery to relax and temporarily paralyze your muscles while a machine breathes for you
It does not put you to sleep or relieve pain by itself - you will also receive anesthesia and pain relief
Tell your anesthetist about kidney problems, muscle diseases (such as myasthenia gravis), and all your medicines, as these can change how long the drug lasts
After surgery you may feel weak or have heavy eyelids briefly as the effect wears off; this is monitored closely
Report any past severe reaction to anesthetic or muscle-relaxant drugs before your procedure
pk: Onset of adequate block within ~2.5-3 minutes after an intubating dose
Elimination half-life approximately 1.5-3 hours (prolonged in renal impairment)
Clinical duration of a long-acting agent, roughly 60-120 minutes depending on dose
Store the lyophilized powder per label; reconstitute before use and use promptly
pearls: Long-acting non-depolarizing aminosteroid blocker with a notably stable cardiovascular profile (minimal vagolysis and little/no histamine release)
Renally eliminated - effect is markedly PROLONGED in renal impairment; avoid or substantially reduce the dose and monitor with train-of-four
Provides NO sedation, amnesia, or analgesia - always give with adequate anesthesia; awareness under paralysis is a hazard if anesthesia is inadequate
Neuromuscular blockade is potentiated by aminoglycosides, magnesium, volatile anesthetics, hypokalemia, hypothermia, and neuromuscular disease
Reverse residual block with neostigmine plus an antimuscarinic, guided by neuromuscular monitoring; never extubate before adequate recovery
The branded product (Arduan) has limited current US marketing; this record reflects FDA/manufacturer and reference labeling for the agent
missed: Not applicable. Pipecuronium is administered only by an anesthesia provider in a controlled setting during a procedure; there is no patient-administered or scheduled outpatient dosing and therefore no missed-dose situation.
overdose: Overdose causes prolonged and profound neuromuscular blockade with respiratory paralysis and apnea, and possible cardiovascular effects. The primary management is to maintain a patent airway and provide controlled mechanical ventilation with oxygen until spontaneous recovery is adequate. Recovery can be hastened, once some spontaneous recovery is evident, by administering an anticholinesterase reversal agent (e.g., neostigmine) together with an antimuscarinic; provide supportive cardiovascular care and monitor with a nerve stimulator.
